title: The Painted Autopsy
premise: Casper Sterling, a night-shift taxi dispatcher in the fading port city of Grayhaven, receives a letter confessing to the murder of his estranged brother Daniel — postmarked a day after Daniel's funeral, where everyone insisted the case was closed as an accidental drowning. The confession names three men who were present that night, all now pillars of the community, and hints at a fourth who 'keeps the paint.' Following the letter's clues through taxi logs, harbor records, and a shuttered body shop, Casper discovers Daniel had been investigating a decades-old cover-up of a dockworker's death, and that the confession itself is bait designed to draw him into finishing what Daniel started. In the climax, Casper corners the surviving conspirators in the flooded undercroft of the old paint factory as the tide rises, forcing a recorded confession; justice arrives not through courts — which one conspirator still owns — but through exposure, exile, and the tide finally surrendering Daniel's missing satchel of evidence.
about_author: August Nystrom is the pen name of a former harbor dispatcher who spent eleven years listening to a city confess itself over the radio, one fare at a time. They write mysteries about ordinary people who know too much and are believed too little.

chapters.title: The Fare Nobody Called
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. A slow night shift at Grayhaven Taxi & Livery: radio chatter, drunks, a silent ride home past the funeral parlor where his brother Daniel lies after a ruling of accidental drowning. Casper skipped the service out of old resentment. The beat is guilt he can't name yet, established through small regrets and the rhythm of the night shift.

chapters.title: Postmarked the Day After
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. A typed letter arrives: 'I killed your brother. Ask the others.' It names three respected men — Councilman Aldous Vey, harbormaster Emil Roark, and Dr. Peter Sallow — and mentions a fourth only as 'the one who keeps the paint.' Postmark dated the day after the funeral. Emotional beat: dread mixed with a shameful flicker of relief that Daniel's death wasn't meaningless.

chapters.title: Closed for Good
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. He takes the letter to Detective Ilsa Brandt, who confirms the drowning case was shut quickly and cleanly — too cleanly, she admits off the record. She warns him that Vey's family practically owns the police pension fund. Beat: the first taste of how power bends institutions; Casper leaves knowing no official help is coming.

chapters.title: The Logbook Habit
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, with flashback texture. Searching grief and habit, he pulls the company's dispatch logs from the night Daniel died and finds a cab dispatched to the old Kestrel Paint Works at 11:40 p.m. — a run never billed, signed out under a driver ID that doesn't exist. Beat: the thrill of the first real thread, and the loneliness of pursuing it alone.

chapters.title: Roark at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins: brief chapters from harbormaster Emil Roark, nervous and watchful. Casper confronts Roark on the pier; Roark denies everything but flinches at the word 'paint.' That night someone keys Casper's car and leaves a second note: STOP ASKING. Beat: fear arrives; the stakes turn physical.

chapters.title: What Daniel Kept
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Going through Daniel's rented room, he finds a hidden notebook: Daniel had been tracing the 1998 death of dockworker Tomas Reyes, ruled an accident, and payments funneled through the paint works. The last page reads: 'If I go in the water, it wasn't the water.' Beat: brotherhood rediscovered too late; grief sharpens into purpose.

chapters.title: Sallow's Steady Hands
chapters.summary: Dr. Sallow's POV. The retired medical examiner drafts and burns another confession letter — revealing he wrote the one Casper received, tormented by conscience but terrified of Vey. Sallow examines his own hands, once so steady. Beat: the antagonist camp fractures; we see guilt has been eating them for twenty-five years.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Drove 44
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. He tracks down Marisol Vega, a former dispatcher who handled the phantom run in 1998 and vanished from the industry afterward. She tells him about the fourth man: Wendell Kestrel, heir to the paint fortune, presumed dead in a boating accident — or living quietly behind the factory walls. Beat: the map of the conspiracy widens; belonging to the city means knowing which stories it agrees to forget.

chapters.title: Vey's Generosity
chapters.summary: Councilman Vey's POV. Vey offers Casper a job, money, and a narrative: Daniel was unstable, obsessed, self-destructive. The offer is silk over a threat. Casper declines. Beat: power shown as seduction before violence; Casper feels the pull of how easy it would be to belong to the winning side.

chapters.title: Arson at the Archive
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. The municipal records annex holding the Reyes file burns overnight. Brandt tips Casper off before the official story hardens, confirming someone inside protects the cover-up. Casper realizes the letter-writer wanted this attention — wanted the fire. Beat: paranoia; every ally might be a lure.

chapters.title: The Letter Writer Speaks
chapters.summary: Anonymous meeting arranged by dead-drop: Sallow, masked, meets Casper in a church confessional booth. He confesses his role in falsifying Reyes's autopsy and Daniel's, insists he sent the letters to force exposure, and gives Casper a key — to a locker at the paint works. Beat: confession as sacrament; justice outside the law begins with truth-telling.

chapters.title: Locker 9
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Inside the locker: Reyes's original autopsy photos, ledgers of payoffs, and a photograph of four young men beside a drum of industrial solvent — Vey, Roark, Sallow, and a fourth face half-turned away. Also, Daniel's spare phone, its last unsent message addressed to Casper: 'Finish it.' Beat: inheritance of a burden; the emotional core of the book.

chapters.title: Roark Breaks
chapters.summary: Roark's POV. Cornered by both Vey's fixer and his own conscience, Roark attempts to flee by boat and instead delivers a partial confession to Casper at gunpoint-of-guilt: they killed Reyes to protect the solvent-dumping scheme, and Daniel died because he found the ledger. Beat: cowardice and complicity; Roark becomes the story's cautionary mirror of Casper.

chapters.title: The Tide Table
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Studying tide charts, Casper realizes the undercroft beneath the paint works floods twice daily — and that Daniel's body was moved through it. The 'accident' scene was staged above, the truth below. He plans to go in during the next low tide. Beat: methodical hope; the detective turns hunter.

chapters.title: Brandt's Choice
chapters.summary: Detective Brandt's POV. Ordered to open a harassment file on Casper, she instead quietly copies the internal-affairs memo implicating Vey in burying the Reyes case, torn between pension and oath. She passes the memo to Casper with the words 'I was never here.' Beat: institutional corruption met by individual integrity; an ally earned, not given.

chapters.title: Into the Undercroft
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. At low tide he enters the flooded undercroft and finds the staging area: chains, a winch, and Daniel's satchel wedged in a grate — but the water is rising faster than the tables promised. Someone has opened the sluice gates. Beat: trap sprung; rising water mirrors rising terror.

chapters.title: The Man Who Keeps the Paint
chapters.summary: Wendell Kestrel's POV. Alive, disfigured by the solvent fire that 'killed' him, Kestrel has lived in the factory for twenty-five years as its ghost-caretaker — the conspiracy's living secret. He reveals he opened the gates not to kill Casper but to flush out Vey, whom he blames for everything, including Daniel's death. Beat: the monster reframed as witness; moral vertigo.

chapters.title: High Water
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Waist-deep, recording on Daniel's phone, Casper gets Kestrel's full testimony just as Vey and his fixer arrive to drown the problem permanently. A brutal struggle in the dark water; Casper nearly drowns, saved when Kestrel turns on Vey's man. Beat: climax — survival bought at cost, evidence secured, loyalties inverted.

chapters.title: What the Courts Can't Hold
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge. Vey's lawyers shred the legality of the recording; the DA declines the case. But Brandt leaks the memo, Marisol goes public, and the recording spreads through the docks like the tide itself. Vey resigns in disgrace; Roark surrenders voluntarily, choosing prison over Vey's protection. Beat: justice outside the law — imperfect, communal, real.

chapters.title: Sallow's Last Autopsy
chapters.summary: Sallow's POV. Facing exposure, Sallow formally retracts both false reports, signs a full confession, and dies peacefully in his sleep the same night — the letter writer's arc complete. Casper attends the quiet funeral, the only mourner besides the priest. Beat: mercy for the repentant; the theme of confession fulfilled.

chapters.title: The Tide Gives Up What It Took
chapters.summary: Casper's POV. Weeks later, at spring low tide, searchers recover Daniel's satchel intact from the grate — the last physical proof, enough for a grand jury against Vey. Casper scatters nothing, keeps everything: Daniel's notebook, the photo, the key. Beat: catharsis; grief given a container at last.

chapters.title: Night Shift, Clear Channel
chapters.summary: Casper's POV, coda. Back on dispatch, the radio quieter now, Casper takes a late fare to the harbor and watches dawn come up over the water that took his brother and gave back the truth. He belongs to Grayhaven fully for the first time — not despite its rot, but because he helped clean some of it. Final beat: belonging earned through witness; the city exhales.
